REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
The Political Reform Act. Many people, groups, and businesses spend money to support or oppose candidates for public office and ballot measures. California's Political Reform Act sets rules for how money can be used in politics and requires public reporting of political spending. These rules apply to state and local candidates, ballot measures, and other public officials, but not to federal candidates or officials. (Federal law establishes campaign finance and reporting requirements for federal offices.) The Political Reform Act has been updated by voters over the years.
Ban on Public Funds to Pay for Campaigns. The Political Reform Act bans the use of public funds for political candidates' campaigns. This ban applies to most elected offices at the state level and local level. (This ban does not apply to city office elections in certain charter cities. Los Angeles, San Francisco, Long Beach, Oakland, and Berkeley are current examples of charter cities that provide public funds to certain campaigns.)
Entities That Oversee Campaign Finance Laws. California's campaign finance laws are administered by the Fair Political Practices Commission and the California Secretary of State. State law requires people and groups to report how much money they give, receive, and spend on political campaigns. This information is available to the public on the Secretary of State's website. The Fair Political Practices Commission enforces and interprets the Political Reform Act. The Fair Political Practices Commission reviews the finance reports and can fine candidates and donors who break the law. The Fair Political Practices Commission issues guidance based on its interpretation of the Political Reform Act.
PROPOSAL
Lifts Ban on Use of Public Funds to Pay for Candidates' Campaigns. Proposition 4 lifts the ban on using public funds for political candidates' campaigns. Removing the ban allows state and local governments to create public campaign financing programs in the future if they wish. Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance system for the state or local governments directly.
Sets Rules for Future State and Local Public Campaign Finance Programs. Proposition 4 sets broad rules for future state and local public campaign finance programs but leaves many key design decisions to future state and local decision makers. Proposition 4 limits which public funds can be used for campaigns, who can receive the funds, and how the funds can be spent in any future public campaign finance program. For example, money meant for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used for campaigns. Candidates can only receive public funds if they show broad-based support in their district and agree to spending limits and other program rules. Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate's personal campaign loan. State and local governments can design and implement their own programs within the broad rules set by Proposition 4.
Fair Political Practices Commission Would Issue Guidance on Public Campaign Finance Programs. Proposition 4 specifies that the Fair Political Practices Commission is not required to administer or enforce local public campaign finance programs. Rather, state and local government officials could ask the Fair Political Practices Commission for guidance on how to create public campaign finance programs consistent with Proposition 4.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Costs of Possible Public Campaign Finance Programs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance program. However, it allows state and local governments to create such programs in the future. The cost of these programs could be significant for governments that choose to create them. The total cost would depend on which governments created such programs and how those programs were designed.
Minor State Costs to Support State and Local Governments Considering Public Campaign Finance Programs. If voters approve Proposition 4, state and local government officials likely would ask the Fair Political Practices Commission for guidance on creating public campaign finance programs under the Political Reform Act. This likely would require the Fair Political Practices Commission to hire more legal staff to help answer these questions. As a result, state costs would be a few hundred thousand dollars each year. This amount is much less than one-tenth of 1 percent (0.1 percent) of the state's total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)

4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 4
YES ON PROPOSITION 4, THE CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT: ELECTIONS SHOULD BE WON, NOT BOUGHT
The amount of money in California elections is outrageous; it's distorting our democracy. Since 2020, more than $1 billion has been spent on California state candidate races alone. This massive spending gives special interests greater access and influence while drowning out the voices of ordinary Californians.
PROP. 4 HELPS QUALIFIED CANDIDATES COMPETE
Running for office today often requires either personal wealth or access to wealthy donors. Deep pockets have become an unofficial requirement to run for office, leaving too many qualified candidates behind.
PROP. 4 CHANGES THE WAY WE FINANCE ELECTION CAMPAIGNS
Programs like small-dollar donation matching help candidates compete without relying on wealthy donors. However, most California communities are banned from using these tools, allowing the influence of big money to grow.
Proposition 4 lifts that ban, giving voters and local governments the option to adopt public financing with strict safeguards so qualified candidates-regardless of their income-can compete against candidates who are backed by wealthy interests.
PROP. 4 BUILDS ON A PROVEN MODEL
We know this reform works because it's working in other states. Thousands of candidates from different backgrounds have been elected in fourteen states and 26 localities using similar systems. They are new people with good ideas from all walks of life. Because they don't rely on wealthy donors, they can speak their mind and work for the people, not the special interests.
PROP. 4 GIVES LOCAL COMMUNITIES A CHOICE
Proposition 4 does not create a public financing program. It simply gives local governments the option to adopt one if they choose.
If a community does, the cost is as little as $1 per resident each year-a small investment to help counter the billions spent influencing California's elections.
PROP. 4 PROTECTS TAXPAYERS
Taxpayer Safeguards:
Requires candidates to meet strict eligibility criteria and abide by spending limits to qualify for public funds.
Prohibits public funding from favoring incumbents or discriminating based on political party.
Prohibits the use of public funds for legal defense or fines.
PROP. 4 CRACKS DOWN ON ILLEGAL FOREIGN MONEY
Proposition 4 triples the maximum fines for illegal foreign campaign contributions and expenditures, strengthening penalties for those who attempt to interfere in California's elections.
PROP. 4 IS SUPPORTED BY LEADERS ACROSS CALIFORNIA
Proposition 4 is backed by a broad coalition including League of Women Voters of California, California Nurses Association, Mental Health Advocacy Services, Social Security Works, California Clean Money Campaign, California Common Cause, California National Organization for Women, Californians for Disability Rights, Consumer Watchdog, Courage California, Democracy for America, Indivisible California: Statestrong, La Defensa, Money Out Voters In, Voters Right to Know, and many others.
PROP. 4 GIVES CALIFORNIANS THE OPPORTUNITY TO RECLAIM THEIR ELECTIONS and ensure they reflect the values of the people, not just the wealthiest donors.
YES ON 4-Restore power to voters, not wealthy donors
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Catherine Kennedy , President
California Nurses Association
Tom Umberg , California State Senator
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 4
Here is what the politicians supporting Proposition 4 do not tell you:
Proposition 4 REPEALS the voter-approved law that PROHIBITS candidates from using taxpayer money to run for office.
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money. In the election last June, more than 60 candidates ran for Governor. Proposition 4 would allow thousands of candidates to get taxpayer money!
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money a candidate can get. Proposition 4 opens the door to taxpayer-funded campaigns but provides no limits on how much taxpayer money a candidate can get and NO LIMIT on spending. It will lead to more negative ads, more junk mail, and more annoying text messages.
Proposition 4 does NOT PROHIBIT SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY in campaigns. Proposition 4 ALLOWS candidates to get taxpayer money AND to get special interest money! Where exactly is the money going to come from to fund thousands of political campaigns? Proposition 4 does not say. But you know the answer. It is coming from YOU, the taxpayers! Less money for schools, less money for public safety, less money for healthcare. More money for politicians.
Proposition 4 is a BLANK CHECK. It is based on false promises and failed solutions.
Proposition 4 does NOT protect taxpayers. That is why Proposition 4 is opposed by California's leading taxpayer organizations.
Proposition 4 does NOT provide for “fair elections.” That is why Proposition 4 is opposed by former Commissioners of the Fair Political Practices Commission.
Vote NO ON PROPOSITION 4.
Robert Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association
Jon Coupal , President
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
Fair Political Practices Commission
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 4
Why did Sacramento politicians put Proposition 4 on the ballot? They want access to YOUR TAXPAYER MONEY to fund THEIR OWN CAMPAIGNS.
Proposition 4 repeals a voter approved law that PROHIBITS these politicians from using public taxpayer funds for their own campaigns. That's right, Proposition 4 allows politicians to use your taxpayer money to fund their campaigns.
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much money they can get! Proposition 4 is a BLANK CHECK. There isn't even a limit on how much they can spend on their campaigns! More negative ads. More junk mail. More annoying text messages. More, more, more.
Proposition 4 is so poorly written, it could allow every state or local “candidate” to get public funding. They don't even have to actually qualify for the ballot to get taxpayer money. Proposition 4 allows for public funding of thousands of state and local candidates. It even allows for public financing of candidates for county political party committees.
In just the last primary election, there were more than 60 candidates for Governor. Do you want YOUR TAXPAYER MONEY going to support more of their negative campaign ads and junk mail?
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money a candidate can receive. It says it requires “strict criteria” to receive taxpayer funds but provides NO DETAILS on what the criteria are! Read the fine print:
“‘Strict criteria' means the requirement set by statute, ordinance, or charter that candidates must meet to receive public funds.”
But there is no current statute, ordinance or charter setting any criteria. Guess who will be setting the criteria? The same politicians who want to get your taxpayer money!
Some good government groups support public financing of campaigns because they want to get special interest money out of politics. BUT PROPOSITION 4 DOES NOT GET RID OF SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY! Under Proposition 4, candidates can raise money from special interests AND get public funding too.
Proposition 4 is the worst kind of public financing scheme. It provides no specifics. It leaves all the details to be worked out by the same politicians who want to get access to public funds.
It is a blank check. But worse than that, Proposition 4 allows special-interest funding of political campaigns.
Please join California's leading taxpayer protection organizations, including the California Taxpayers Association, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California, United Latinos Action, as well as former members of California's Fair Political Practices Commission, who all oppose Proposition 4.
PLEASE VOTE NO ON THE POLITICIANS' BLANK CHECK PROPOSITION. VOTE NO ON PROP. 4.
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
Fair Political Practices Commission
Colleen McAndrews , Former Commissioner
Fair Political Practices Commission
Julian Canete , President
California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 4
DON'T BE MISLED BY SPECIAL INTERESTS WHO WANT TO KEEP BUYING ELECTIONS
California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns. Communities in all 49 other states have the right to adopt public financing to allow qualified candidates to compete against wealthy donors. California doesn't. Prop. 4 simply removes that ban and gives local voters the same choice everyone else has, while instituting strict taxpayer safeguards.
PROP. 4 GIVES POWER BACK TO LOCAL COMMUNITIES AND EMPOWERS VOTERS, NOT DONORS
Prop. 4 doesn't spend a single taxpayer dollar or institute public financing anywhere. It simply removes the ban to give every city, county, and the state the right to adopt public funding if local voters want it. The details are appropriately left to each community. But any system MUST require candidates to abide by spending limits and demonstrate broad-based support in their district to qualify.
PROP. 4 MAKES ELECTED OFFICIALS ACCOUNTABLE TO VOTERS, NOT DONORS
Corporate special interests oppose Prop. 4 because public financing allows candidates to run and win without relying on them-threatening their grip on California elections.
Thousands of candidates from different backgrounds have been elected across the country using public financing, for a tiny cost. Because they don't rely on wealthy donors, they can speak their minds and work for the people, not special interests.
DON'T BE FOOLED BY CORPORATE SPECIAL INTERESTS HIDING BEHIND NICE-SOUNDING NAMES.
VOTE YES ON 4 to let local voters and communities reclaim their elections so they're won, not bought.
Carmen Balber , Executive Director
Consumer Watchdog
Camerina Davidson , President
California National Organization for Women
Darius Kemp , Executive Director
California Common Cause

OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Current law prohibits state and local governments from using public funds for election campaigns except in charter cities and counties.
This measure repeals that prohibition and allows state and local governments to establish public campaign financing programs for candidates who agree to specified spending limits and meet eligibility criteria.
Prohibits public funding programs from using funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
Prohibits candidates from using public funds for legal defense costs, fines, or repayment of personal loans to campaigns.
Triples maximum fine for campaign contributions by foreign entities.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs.

S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 6, 2026
Americans don’t agree on much in today’s hyperpolarized climate. But they overwhelmingly believe that money is a corrupting influence in politics.
According to a 2023 Pew Research poll (https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/09/19/the-biggest-problems-and-greatest-strengths-of-the-u-s-political-system/), 85% of respondents said they thought the cost of mounting a campaign deters “good people” from running for office, and 84% said wealthy special interests and lobbyists exercise too much sway over politics.
Unfortunately, systemic reform to our campaign finance system is incredibly difficult. The 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Citizens United struck down limits on independent political spending by corporations and labor unions.
But could California carve its own path to reducing money in politics?

That’s what backers of Proposition 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which Democratic state lawmakers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) placed on the November ballot, contend their measure will do.
Prop 4 would overturn California’s ban on public campaign financing — in place since voters approved Prop 73 in 1988 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_73,_Funds_for_Election_Campaigns_Initiative_(June_1988)) — and give local and state governments the option of providing taxpayer funding for candidates’ political campaigns.
Supporters argue this will dilute the influence of special interests while making elected officials more accountable to voters — and leveling the playing field and encouraging more diverse, nonincumbent and first-time candidates.
That certainly sounds good, but is there meaningful research to back it up?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A natural place to look is California’s charter cities, which are exempt from the public financing ban; seven have programs (https://www.commoncause.org/california/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/CA-Municipal-Index-Reportv7-Final_Authored.pdf). San Francisco, Berkeley, Los Angeles, Sacramento and Long Beach provide matching funds to eligible candidates who receive a certain level of small-dollar donations; Oakland gives residents “democracy vouchers” they can donate to candidates and Richmond offers grants to candidates each time they reach a new fundraising tier.
How well have these programs been working?
Unfortunately, no one really knows. There hasn’t been much academic research into any of the programs, let alone a rigorous cross-comparison of them.
Despite a wealth of information on San Francisco’s public financing program — captured in an annual report from the city ethics commission — the data has yet to be thoroughly studied. Indeed, the overworked commission refers to its report as “primarily descriptive” (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2023/05/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-november-8-2022-election.html) and practically begs for a “more comprehensive analysis” of the program — noting that (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2025/03/san-francisco-public-campaign-financing-program-report-for-the-november-5-2024-election.html) certain “labor-intensive” and “paperwork-heavy” aspects are “ineffective.”
Meanwhile, the studies that do exist suggest there’s a lot of room for improvement.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A 2013 examination of Oakland’s program (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) found “no evidence” that it reduced the influence of wealthy donors, spurred more candidates to run or increased voter turnout, although it appears to have made certain races more competitive and shrunk incumbents’ margin of victory. And a 2017 peer-reviewed study (https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/for-2017-0015/html) comparing New York City’s and Los Angeles’ public financing programs found that L.A.’s program design made it “substantially less effective” than New York’s.
All available research indicates that the effectiveness of a public campaign finance program depends enormously on how it’s designed.
Yet Prop 4 ignores best practices and imposes no meaningful checks on bad policies.
It gives local and state governments broad discretion to design programs, as long as they follow a few basic rules: To receive public funds, candidates would have to demonstrate “broad-based” community support — such as receiving a certain amount of small-dollar donations — and agree to abide by spending limits. They couldn’t use public funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety — or use public money to repay personal loans to their campaign or cover legal defense fees.
“Cities are the laboratory of democracy … We wanted to give maximum freedom to jurisdictions,” Trent Lange, executive director of the California Clean Money Action Fund and co-chair of the Yes on Prop 4 campaign, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But we’ve been running these experiments for years. The labs are in operation, but no one has bothered to gather the data or review the research.
And we have significant concerns about letting state and local governments run wild with taxpayer money — especially in the dark.
True, Prop 4 has some protections. The ban on using public funds to pay legal defense fees, for example, is aimed at closing the Eric Swalwell loophole: The disgraced Democratic ex-U.S. representative used hundreds of thousands of dollars from his California gubernatorial campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/eric-swalwell-campaign-payments-22362761.php) to pay for his legal defense against multiple sexual-assault allegations.
But such protections are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop 4 offers no guarantee they will be.
In fact, it explicitly exempts the state’s respected campaign finance watchdog, the California Fair Political Practices Commission, from administering or enforcing local public financing programs.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Nor does the measure require local governments to set up their own watchdog agencies — even though Lange acknowledged “a public financing system needs a good oversight board.”
That’s a recipe for disaster.
Without San Francisco’s ethics commission, for example, 2024 mayoral candidate Mark Farrell — who received $1.2 million in public funds (https://sfethics.org/ethics/2026/03/campaign-finance-audit-report-mark-farrell-for-mayor-2024-id-1466726.html) — might have gotten away with illegally using funds (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/mark-farrell-hit-ethics-fine-eve-of-mayor-election-19886013.php) from a separate ballot-measure campaign to subsidize his mayoral campaign (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/mark-farrell-campaign-finance-19654509.php).
We understand Prop 4 proponents’ hesitation to be overly prescriptive — San Francisco’s ridiculously clunky charter is the result of years of unnecessary regulations and stipulations being written into ballot measures.
But the details missing from Prop 4 aren’t ancillary. As the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office observed (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop4-110326.pdf), the measure leaves “many key design decisions” up to state and local lawmakers, who could directly benefit from the programs they create.
Consider the requirement that candidates abide by spending limits if they accept public funds. That sounds great, but Prop 4 doesn’t include guardrails for what a meaningful cap would be — and some local governments clearly need guardrails.
Thomas Hiltachk, a lawyer who frequently works on ballot measures and opposes Prop 4, cited the Los Angeles County city of Inglewood, which in 2020 capped local campaign contributions at the absurd amount of $100,000 per person (https://www.dailybreeze.com/2020/11/24/inglewood-caps-campaign-contributions-at-100000-to-avoid-new-state-law/) — 21 times the statewide max of $4,700.
This isn’t to say that public campaign financing is inherently a bad idea. We’ve supported the idea in the past (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-California-deserves-more-campaign-12165476.php), including a 2016 Berkeley pilot program (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-Yes-on-Measure-X1-9984435.php).
But we can’t get behind a measure that doesn’t require local and state governments to adhere to any established best practices. This is a fatal flaw that opens the door to limited taxpayer funds being wasted on efforts that don’t meaningfully move the needle — at a time of widespread budget deficits.

There’s no excuse for Prop 4’s backers’ failure to do this homework, given that voters rejected efforts to lift California’s ban on public campaign financing in 2000 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/25_03_2000.html), 2006 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2006/89_11_2006.htm) and 2010 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2010/15_06_2010.aspx).

How to vote on California’s Proposition 4: McClatchy Media’s recommendation | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 2, 2026 4:49 PM
"I voted" stickers await voters at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. Proposition 4 would repeal California’s ban on public financing of political campaigns.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Of the 14 propositions on California’s November ballot, Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html) could be one of the least accessible to the average voter.
Here is what you need to know: A “Yes” vote on Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on the use of tax dollars to fund local and state elections.
“The measure (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=4&year=2026) would allow state and local governments to create programs for the use of certain public funds to finance political campaigns,” wrote The Bee last week. “Candidates would be prohibited from using the funds to repay personal loans to their campaigns, legal defense fees or fines. Those who receive public funds would be required to show broad-based local support and pledge their compliance with spending limits and other rules.”
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html)
Public money set aside for education, transportation or public safety would not be available to be used for local and state elections. “Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate’s personal campaign loan,” wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
“We just want to lift the ban, putting into place certain reasonable, common-sense taxpayer requirements so that communities have the opportunity to use public financing to allow qualified candidates the chance to run,” said Trent Lange, president and executive director of the California Clean Money Campaign.
Other groups in favor of Prop. 4 include the California Democratic Party, ACLU California Action (https://aclucalaction.org/2026-election-guide/), California Clean Money Action Fund, End Citizens United and the League of Women Voters of California, as well as state senators Ben Allen, D-Santa Monica; Sabrina Cervantes, D-Riverside; and Tom Umberg, D-Villa Park. Those in opposition are the California Republican Party, Reform California and California Taxpayers Association.
The editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/)Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) recommend a “Yes” vote on Prop. 4. The measure would end the state’s overly restrictive ban on public financing of campaigns. Public financing amplifies the voices of everyday voters and gives candidates an alternative to relying on wealthy donors.
A “Yes” vote would allow local governments to create matching-fund programs, in which public money matches small private donations, or public campaign-grant programs that provide qualifying candidates with a set amount of taxpayer money. Such programs would reduce candidates’ dependence on large donors and political committees, lower barriers to running for office, and help build a more diverse and representative democracy.
“Everybody knows that the amount of money in politics is outrageous, and it’s corrupting our democracy,” Lange told the board.
“All that money buys access for special interests while shutting out the rest of us. We believe that we need to change the way we finance election campaigns so that elected officials can focus on working for the people, rather than their big-money donors.”

With 14 statewide ballot measures on the ballot, Proposition 4 is thankfully simple to understand.
If approved, Prop. 4 will repeal California’s general ban on public funding of campaigns and allow most cities and the state to establish public-financing programs if they so choose. That ban was enacted by voters as part of Proposition 73 in 1988, which sought to constrain the use of tax dollars in elections.
As proponents of Prop. 73, including the late Joel Fox, argued at the time in proposing the ban on public funding of campaigns: “Keeping government spending under control is hard enough. Imagine how much harder it will be to keep politicians from spending more tax money on the most important thing in their lives — getting elected and reelected.”
Such concerns are perhaps the chief reason to leave the ban in place.
While Prop. 73’s ban applies to the state and general law cities, charter cities — those operating under their own local constitution, or charter — are allowed to authorize public financing of campaigns if they choose to. Out of the 126 charter cities in the state, only Los Angeles, San Francisco, Oakland, Berkeley, and Long Beach have authorized such programs. However, Oakland’s “Democracy Dollars” program, while officially approved in 2022, has been postponed due to fiscal challenges in the city.
Proponents of such systems argue that such systems help rebalance the scales in local elections often dominated by special interests with deep pockets. Empirical evidence on the impact of such systems is limited, but some research has found such systems are associated (https://www.jstor.org/stable/27369278) with more candidates entering races and spending less time (https://campaignlegal.org/sites/default/files/Public%20Financing%20Fact%20Sheet.pdf) on fundraising.
As a real-world example, former Los Angeles Times opinion editor Mariel Garza notes (https://goldenstatereport.substack.com/p/a-post-citizens-united-world-needs), “Los Angeles’ public financing system provides a 6:1 match and likely helped Karen Bass win the mayor’s race in 2022 against her wealthy challenger, shopping-mall developer Rick Caruso.” In other words, the system simply replaced private funds with taxpayer dollars to tip the scales for an establishment political careerist over a private-sector outsider. Make of that what you will.

If there were more obvious benefits of such systems, one would expect to see broader implementation of them. Charter cities remain an option for experimentation, for better or worse. But it’s not obvious there’s a need to give a greenlight to every city in the state, or the state itself, to hand out taxpayer dollars to political campaigns.
Voters are indeed skeptical of Prop. 4, according to recent polling (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) from the Public Policy Institute of California, which found that just 42% of likely voters support it while 53% are opposed, with the balance undecided. This includes the support of just 47% of people from the Los Angeles area and just 41% from the San Francisco Bay area.
Straightforwardly, Prop. 4 just doesn’t pass the common sense test. At a time when governments across the state are hemorrhaging money and turning to tax increases to sustain the services they currently have, why even allow politicians to set up programs giving tax dollars to their campaigns and the campaigns of their friends? While we’re sure politicians would prefer to spend less time fundraising, does that justify diverting finite tax dollars away from things that will directly benefit taxpayers?
If charter cities want to keep experimenting, fine, that’s already allowed. But should we lift the ban on public funding of campaigns across the state? We don’t think so.
Vote no on Prop. 4.

I'm noting the SF Chronicle's key claims: public financing has no meaningful research backing in California, and a 2013 Oakland study found no evidence it cut donor influence or raised turnout, though it did make some races more competitive. Now I'm turning to a 2017 peer-reviewed comparison of New York City and Los Angeles.

Now I'm going through the Chronicle's remaining points: the 2017 study's finding that design drives results, the critique that Prop 4 leaves design to local governments, and the FPPC's exclusion from local administration. Then I'm moving on to the Sacramento Bee's case, its endorsements, and the groups on each side.

Now I'm weighing the Press-Enterprise's case: the ban was put in place to protect tax dollars, and it says those concerns are likely the main reason to keep it. It also notes that research on candidate entry and fundraising time is limited, and it questions whether LA's matching funds helped Karen Bass win. I want to check the PPIC poll numbers, which show 42% support and 53% opposition among likely voters.

Now I'm looking at what supporters could point to: research on programs like New York City's matching system and Maine, Arizona, and Connecticut's Clean Elections, plus the costs local governments would bear.

Now I'm checking whether the measure's increased-limits trigger could run into First Amendment problems, the way Arizona's matching funds provision did in the 2011 Bennett decision.

Now I'm checking the measure's expenditure-limit trigger, which lets limits rise based on opponents' private spending and independent expenditures. That looks a lot like the Arizona matching-funds provision the Court struck down in Bennett, since it penalizes privately financed candidates by channeling public money to their rivals.

Now I'm checking whether the measure's expenditure-limit trigger could run into First Amendment problems, since a limit that rises with opponents' private spending looks like the equalizing scheme the Court struck down in Davis v. FEC. I want to see whether any source raises that issue, and whether the Bennett decision on Arizona's matching funds applies here.

Now I'm planning to check the Berkeley IGS guide for its summary of the arguments, along with the LAO analysis for any legal risk notes. I also want to see whether the LA Times editorial board has taken a position, and whether Governor Newsom has said anything about Prop 4 despite signing SB 42.

Now I'm planning to check the official fund-contribution totals for the Prop 4 committees, then confirm the PPIC poll numbers and look at the Berkeley IGS summary and LAO analysis for fiscal details.

Next I'm working through a list of follow-up checks: the Berkeley IGS guide, the PPIC poll on Prop 4, CalMatters and LA Times coverage, research on public financing outcomes in cities and states, and any legal risk from the Bennett decision.

Now I'm running through the remaining checks: the constitutional question, a look at the 2016 SB 1107 ruling for background, the cost claim of about $1 per resident, and who is funding each side.

content.text: The editorial boards split: the Chronicle and Press-Enterprise say no, while the Bee and several other papers say yes. I'll check the polling, the Berkeley guide, and whether any news outlet has done neutral reporting.

Proposition 4: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding
Proposition 4: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding
Proposition 4: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns. Legislative Statute.
Additional Titles
Public Fundraising, Allow Public Financing of Election Campaigns Measure
Summary
Proposition 4 was placed on the ballot by Senate Bill 42 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) (SB 42). SB 42 changes provisions of the Political Reform Act of 1974, which bans the use of public funds for candidates’ political campaigns. The senate passed the bill in June 2025, with the Assembly passing it in September 2025. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the bill in October, sending it to the ballot as Proposition 4.
Proposition 4 would remove California’s prohibition on using public money to finance political candidates, allowing state and local governments to establish publicly funded campaign programs in the future. The measure would not itself create such a program, but would give governments the option to develop their own systems within statewide guidelines.
Under the measure, funds dedicated to purposes such as education, transportation, and public safety could not be redirected to campaigns. Candidates receiving public financing would have to demonstrate a sufficient level of support among voters and comply with spending limits and other program requirements. Public funds could not be used for legal defense costs, fines, or repayment of a candidate’s personal campaign loans. State and local governments would determine the details of their individual programs, while the Fair Political Practices Commission (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/) could provide guidance on complying with Proposition 4 but would not be required to administer or enforce local programs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 4 would not automatically require new spending because it does not establish a public campaign financing program. Costs would arise only if the state or local governments later choose to create such programs, with the amount depending on how widely they are adopted and how they are structured. The state would also likely spend a few hundred thousand dollars annually for additional Fair Political Practices Commission (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/) staff to advise governments on developing programs that comply with the measure.
What your vote means
Yes: A “yes” vote would end the statewide ban on public campaign financing, allowing state and local governments to establish programs that provide public funds to qualifying candidates under specified rules and spending limits.
No: A “no” vote would maintain the existing prohibition on public financing of campaigns, including the current exception for certain charter cities.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 4 would reduce the influence of wealthy donors and special interests by allowing state and local governments to establish public campaign financing programs. They say these programs could help qualified candidates compete for office without relying heavily on wealthy donors, while requiring participating candidates to meet eligibility requirements and spending limits. Proposition 4 would also prohibit using funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety and would strengthen penalties for illegal foreign campaign contributions.
Opponents argue that Proposition 4 could allow taxpayer money to be used to fund political campaigns without setting specific limits on how much public funding candidates could receive. They contend that important details are not included, leaving many key decisions to future state and local decision makers. Critics note that candidates receiving public funds could still accept private and special-interest contributions, meaning the measure would not eliminate private money from campaigns.

Should California taxpayers chip in to fund political campaigns? Prop. 4 lets you decide
by
Yue Stella Yu (https://calmatters.org/author/yue-yu/)

In summary
Prop. 4 would lift a ban that prohibits state and most local candidates from using public funding for their political campaigns. Proponents argue the mechanism helps more candidates run for office, but opponents are skeptical.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
In 1988, a Democrat, a Republican and an independent in the state Legislature co-authored a ballot measure to ban most political campaigns from using public money.
Their rationale? There was already too much money in politics.
“It certainly makes no sense to open the biggest money source of all, the taxpayers’ purses and wallets,” proponents argued (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1988&context=ca_ballot_props). Nearly 60% of voters agreed.
Almost four decades later, some good-government groups argue that the state needs to do the exact opposite to counter the influence of money in politics.
They, along with the state Democratic Party, are backing Proposition 4 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-4-public-fundraising/) on the November ballot, which would lift the 1988 ban and authorize the state and most local governments to set up public campaign financing systems for state and local races.
Seven charter cities in California, including San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland, were spared from the 1988 ban and already have public campaign financing.
To qualify for the funding, candidates must meet criteria such as proving they have a certain number of small donors or agreeing to cap how much they raise and spend on their campaign. Depending on the city, eligible candidates receive the funding as a grant, a matching fund indexed to their total donations, or a voucher voters can give to campaigns.
Proponents of Prop. 4 may face an uphill battle: Voters have twice rejected similar ballot measures to lift the ban, and public polling so far suggests voters are skeptical.
What supporters, opponents say
Elections have gotten more expensive over the past three decades, both federally and statewide.
In 2000, federal candidates, parties and special interests spent $5.6 billion on congressional and presidential races. By 2020, that number had nearly quadrupled to $18 billion (https://www.opensecrets.org/elections-overview/cost-of-election?display=T), according to OpenSecrets, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that tracks campaign spending nationwide.
In California, special interests spent $26 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2025/10/prop50-money-ads-mailers-billboards/) running competing ads on redistricting last year, making it the most expensive ballot measure race in state history. This year, California had the most expensive governor’s race (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/03/us/elections/california-governor-campaign-finance.html) in U.S. history, with billionaire Tom Steyer pouring $213 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-rich-candidates-funding-elections/) of his own money into his unsuccessful gubernatorial bid.
Supporters of Prop. 4 say public campaign financing is necessary as a check against that kind of unfettered private campaign spending, because candidates often must accept campaign spending limits to qualify for public funding. They say public financing will lead to more diverse candidates by attracting those who otherwise couldn’t afford to run for office.

“We need to change the way we finance election campaigns so candidates can run and win without having to raise big money, and they can spend their time listening to voters rather than their donors,” said Trent Lange, president of California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes on Prop. 4 campaign.
Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) and the Democratic-led state Legislature, which voted last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb42) to place Prop. 4 on the November ballot, also support the measure. Sen. Tom Umberg (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/thomas-umberg-165043), a Santa Ana Democrat and a co-author of Prop. 4, said it would help alleviate a “growing cynicism in politics” and allow candidates to spend more time developing policies instead of fundraising.
“To the extent that we can engage particularly small donors, that will … empower and also engage the body politic, particularly young people,” he said.
But opponents say politicians should not use taxpayer dollars (https://caltax.org/prop4/) to run campaigns. They argue the measure would force voters to subsidize candidates they otherwise wouldn’t support, and that fraudulent candidates could exploit the system.
Voters have previously rejected ballot initiatives that would have allowed public money to be used for political campaigns. Nearly two-thirds of voters shot down a 2000 measure that would have allowed candidates to tap public funds for advertising (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/25_03_2000.html). In 2010, 58% of voters opposed a 2010 measure (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_15,_Biennial_Lobbyist_Fee_and_Public_Campaign_Funding_Measure_(June_2010)) to lift the 1988 ban.
“The voters have been quite clear they don’t want taxpayer money being used for politics,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican, said last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/278290#t=221&f=fe479f37ee7a3df6888379e9be069fd8) on the Assembly floor. “Unfortunately, politicians simply can’t take no for an answer.”

Critics also doubt the effectiveness of Prop. 4, arguing it is not specific enough to have teeth.
Prop. 4 offers only broad instructions to local governments and the state. It would ban candidates from using public funds meant for education, public safety and transportation. It would require candidates to prove they have enough public support and to agree to certain spending limits to receive funding, but doesn’t spell out how much. It would also ban candidates from using the money to pay for legal defenses, fines or personal loans to their campaigns.
The measure specifically exempts the Fair Political Practices Commission, the state’s campaign finance watchdog, from ensuring local programs are not exploited or abused, leaving it largely to local governments. But not every local government has its own watchdog agency, let alone an effective one.
The San Francisco Chronicle’s editorial board, in opposing Prop. 4, argued that its rules “are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop. 4 offers no guarantee they will be.”
Effectiveness debate
Fifteen states and Washington, D.C., offer some sort of statewide public financing for political campaigns, according to an analysis by the National Conference of State Legislatures (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/public-financing-of-campaigns-overview).
Studies are mixed on the effectiveness of those programs.
Some, including one in 2003 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1532673X03256784) by two University of Maryland scholars, suggest that candidates who accept public financing spend less time fundraising, freeing them up for other campaign activities.
Some researchers found that public financing expanded the pool of candidates running for office. A 2022 study of Seattle’s program (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0047272722000780), which gives each registered voter four $25 vouchers to contribute to the campaign of their choice, concluded that the program boosted the number of candidates by 86%. Another study (https://web.stanford.edu/~neilm/The%20Impact%20of%20Public%20Financing%20on%20Electoral%20Competition.pdf) of Arizona and Maine’s programs found that they “significantly increased competition.”
Others disagreed. The United States Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan research agency advising Congress, studied Arizona and Maine’s programs (https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-10-390.pdf) in 2010 and concluded there was no evidence that public financing led to more candidates.
There’s little evidence that public financing has curbed the influence of private donors, according to the Seattle study and the GAO report.
In California, few studies have examined the effectiveness of local programs. A 2023 San Francisco Ethics Commission study found candidates have increasingly tapped into the public funds and that third-party spending was “at near all-time lows.” But the commission encouraged a more comprehensive analysis. A 2013 study (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) in Oakland found no evidence its program diluted the influence of wealthy donors, although it did seem to boost competition.
Researchers point to the difficulty (https://sgp.jhu.edu/primers/public-funding-of-us-elections/#conclusion) of studying public financing programs, because most apply in only a handful of states and it is hard to measure what would have happened if the programs had not been in place.
The lack of compelling evidence makes Prop. 4 proponents’ claims shaky, the San Diego Union-Tribune’s editorial board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/endorsement-dont-buy-prop-4s-baloney-about-publicly-financed-campaigns/) argued.
“So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits,” it said.
The ballot measure should not be overly prescriptive, said Dora Rose, deputy director for the League of Women Voters of California, a co-sponsor of Prop. 4.
“Prop. 4 sets basic safeguards and then lets communities learn from the evidence and decide what works for them,” she said.
For now, voters appear skeptical. A September poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the Public Policy Institute of California found 53% of likely voters would oppose Prop. 4, while just 42% would vote yes. Another poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf) by the UC-Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies shows a tighter matchup, with 35% of likely voters supporting the measure and another 35% against it.

Allow public financing of political campaigns
This would authorize California’s state and local governments to establish public campaign funds for candidates if they choose to. It would reverse a 1988 ban on such systems for the state and most local governments. Currently, only five California cities have public financing for local offices, including Berkeley and San Francisco. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.

content.thinking:
I'm reviewing the CalMatters explainer, noting that the Seattle study found vouchers raised the number of candidates by 86%, while the Arizona and Maine evidence showed more competition. The GAO's 2010 finding was that public financing didn't clearly produce more candidates in those states, and there's little sign it reduced private donor influence. Oakland's 2013 program showed no evidence of diluted influence.

I'm checking the endorsement lists against the CalMatters article, and I notice the Press-Enterprise isn't in its list even though the Mercury News is. Next I want to verify the PPIC and UC Berkeley poll numbers from September.

I'm pulling up the PPIC October poll on Prop 4, which I've seen reported as 45% yes and 52% no, to confirm those numbers on the official survey page. I also want to check the Seattle study's 86% candidate increase against a source beyond CalMatters, and look for any legal challenges to the expenditure-limit formula under Bennett.

Next I'm going to check the Mercury News editorial against the others, then look at the official PPIC October numbers and the Ballotpedia summary. I also want to see how much money each side has raised, and whether anyone has challenged the expenditure-limit formula in court.

content.text: CalMatters gives a balanced read of the research: some studies show more candidates, others find little effect, and the evidence on curbing donor influence is thin. I'll check the latest polling, the campaign money, and any legal-risk analysis.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . content.thinking:
Now I'm noting the latest PPIC October poll on Prop 4: 45% yes and 52% no, up from 42% and 53% in September. Partisan support is 60% among Democrats, 22% among Republicans, and 42% among independents, with only the Bay Area reaching a majority at 51%. I'm also starting to pull the campaign finance figures for the Yes side through 10/22, where contributions so far total $984,699.

The Yes committees have reported about $985K in contributions, with most of it from the main Yes on 4 committee. As of October 22, the SOS listing shows no identified No committee, even though CalTax and HJTA are campaigning against it. That gap in reported funding may matter less than the poll numbers, so I'll mention it briefly.

Now I'm looking for legal analysis of Prop 4's constitutionality, along with the LA Times editorial position and the San Diego Union-Tribune critique, and checking the Seattle voucher study's 86% figure.

In 2008, the Institute for Justice and the Goldwater Institute teamed up to challenge Arizona’s punitive system of funding campaigns with taxpayer money.
The consolidated challenges to the “matching funds” provision of Arizona’s so-called “Clean Elections” Act eventually made their way to the U.S. Supreme Court, which on March 28, 2011, heard argument in
*Arizona Free Enterprise Club’s Freedom Club PAC v.
Bennett* (No. 10-238) and *McComish v.Bennett* (No. 10-239).
The cases sought to vindicate the rights of independent political groups and candidates who did not take taxpayer funds to speak freely during political campaigns without having the government attempt to “level the playing field.”
Under the Arizona law, if a group made an independent expenditure in favor of a privately financed candidate, the unelected bureaucrats at the Clean Elections Commission doled out an almost dollar-for-dollar amount of “matching funds” to the publicly funded candidate.
That meant that for every dollar a group or individual spent to support the candidate of their choice, over the publicly funded candidate’s initial government subsidy, the government paid an equal amount of money to the political competition.
The Ninth Circuit, in conflict with controlling Supreme Court precedent and contrary to decisions from other federal appellate courts, found this system to be constitutional.

# California Voters Will Choose Whether to Allow Public Campaign Financing — Here’s Why It Matters
This November, California voters will decide whether to adopt Proposition 4, a ballot measure that would allow the state to enact public campaign financing programs.
...
Public financing programs currently exist in at least 14 states and 26 localities, including five California charter cities, but state law currently bans other localities and the state from creating similar programs.
Prop 4 would repeal that ban, giving the legislature and local governments the opportunity to create new public financing programs.
...
One of the most effective and best-studied systems is small donor matching, which matches small donations from individuals in the community with public funds.
Los Angeles, Berkeley, Long Beach, and San Francisco use this model, as do New York State and New York City.
Other programs, including statewide systems in Arizona, Connecticut, and Maine, offer qualifying candidates block grants.
Another model provides eligible voters with vouchers that they can use to assign public funds to participating candidates, as Oakland will soon do.
Prop 4 does not require the state or any locality to adopt any of these systems, or to enact public financing at all.
It simply gives them the option.

I'm noting that the LA Times columnist backs Prop 4, while the editorial board's position is unclear, and that Newsom listed it as a Yes in his October 9 slate. I also want to check the Brennan Center's analysis for its arguments and any comments on constitutionality, and I'm starting to look at the Bennett decision.

I'm now checking how the Bennett ruling applies to Prop 4's clause that raises expenditure limits based on opponents' spending, and whether it resembles the matching-funds scheme the Court struck down. I'm also weighing it against Davis v. FEC, which struck down a rule that burdened one candidate's speech to favor another.

I'm worried that the Bennett and Davis reasoning could expose Prop 4's expenditure-limit increase to a First Amendment challenge, since it's permissive and each jurisdiction would set its own limits. I'll describe that as my own reading and cite the precedents as context. I still want to see whether the Brennan Center addresses how the measure handles Bennett.

I'm planning to pull the Brennan Center article for its pro-measure evidence, plus the San Diego Union-Tribune editorial for the opposing case and the JHU public-financing primer for a more neutral summary of the evidence. I'll also check the Yes campaign's FAQ for its key claims.

California Voters Will Choose Whether to Allow Public Campaign Financing — Here’s Why It Matters
Public financing is the most effective counter we have to the influence of megadonors in politics.

This November, California voters will decide whether to adopt Proposition 4 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/index.htm), a ballot measure that would allow the state to enact public campaign financing programs. Approving the measure would be a powerful way to counter the corrupting influence of big money in state politics. It would allow candidates to run competitive campaigns without depending on large donors and help more Californians engage meaningfully with the political process.
California elections are awash in money. In the 2026 primary elections, outside groups representing some of the state's wealthiest individuals and most powerful business interests spent $9 million (https://www.loscerritosnews.net/2026/05/29/money-floods-ad-67-race-9-million-in-outside-spending-turns-local-assembly-contest-into-proxy-war/) to influence just one assembly district seat. Several billionaires and billionaire-fueled PACs poured (https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jun/01/tech-billionaires-california-elections) millions into other state legislative races that in the past would have been community-focused contests. These developments mirror a larger national trend in which a handful of ultra-wealthy donors increasingly dominate election spending. And this year's midterms are on track (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/07/extraordinary-amount-money-pouring-into-midterm-elections/) to break spending records, with the top 50 donors (https://www.washingtonpost.com/elections/interactive/2026/06/25/these-are-biggest-individual-donors-2026-election-cycle/) already having poured nearly $1.8 billion into the election. That figure doesn't include an additional reported $276 million (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/us/politics/elon-musk-midterms.html) spent by Elon Musk.
Thanks to Citizens United and other court decisions, states and localities cannot limit how much billionaires and wealthy industries like AI, crypto, and hedge funds spend on California elections. But they can provide alternative ways for candidates to reach voters.
One of the most powerful is to provide voluntary public financing for candidates who have demonstrated viability. Public financing programs currently exist (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/guide-public-financing-programs-nationwide) in at least 14 states and 26 localities, including five California charter cities, but state law (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/about-fppc/about-the-political-reform-act/) currently bans other localities and the state from creating similar programs. Prop 4 would repeal that ban, giving the legislature and local governments the opportunity to create new public financing programs.
They would have a number of models to choose from. One of the most effective and best-studied systems is small donor matching, which matches small donations from individuals in the community with public funds. Los Angeles (https://ethics.lacity.gov/publications/matching-funds-faq-2026/), Berkeley (https://berkeleyca.gov/your-government/elections/campaign-finance), Long Beach (https://library.municode.com/ca/long_beach/codes/municipal_code?nodeId=TIT2ADPE_CH2.01THLOBECAREAC), and San Francisco (https://sfethics.org/guidance/campaigns/candidates/public-financing-program) use this model, as do New York State and New York City. Other programs, including statewide systems in Arizona, Connecticut, and Maine, offer qualifying candidates block grants. Another model provides eligible voters with vouchers that they can use to assign public funds to participating candidates, as Oakland (https://www.oaklandca.gov/Government/Boards-Commissions/Public-Ethics-Commission/Democracy-Dollars-Program) will soon do. Prop 4 does not require the state or any locality to adopt any of these systems, or to enact public financing at all. It simply gives them the option.
Some who oppose (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-prop-4-public-financing-22426379.php) Prop 4 argue that California's existing public financing programs need further study before expanding the reform in the state. But Prop 4 does not create any new programs - it simply gives the state and localities more options. Jurisdictions across the state that want to implement public financing would still be able to weigh the pros and cons while looking to especially strong models, like New York State, as they develop their own programs.
The benefits of public financing in New York and elsewhere are in fact well-documented. Data from New York State's first cycle (https://pcfb.ny.gov/system/files/documents/2025/01/2024-new-york-state-public-campaign-finance-board-election-cycle-report-final.pdf) of public financing in 2024 shows a remarkable shift (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/new-york-states-public-campaign-financing-program-empowers-constituent) in campaign funding. Publicly financed candidates relied significantly more on small, in-district contributions than in past elections. Roughly twice as many (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/new-york-states-public-campaign-financing-program-empowers-constituent) New Yorkers made small-dollar donations compared to the 2020 or 2022 cycles. The increase in small donations was driven by local constituents, which is striking in a state where out-of-district and out-of-state donors have historically dominated (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/new-york-states-public-campaign-financing-program-empowers-constituent) election giving.
Other jurisdictions have had similar successes. In DC's (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/major-strides-public-campaign-financing) first citywide elections with public financing in 2020, publicly financed candidates tended to outraise and enjoy greater electoral success than their privately financed counterparts. In Seattle, the number of residents donating to city campaigns more than doubled (https://www.seattle.gov/documents/Departments/EthicsElections/DemocracyVoucher/Program%20Data/Reports/2021%20Seattle%20Democracy%20Voucher%20Report.pdf?inline=1) in just the first few years that public financing was available. And after Berkeley, California's public financing program went into effect in 2018, contributions from non-Berkeley residents dropped (https://maplightarchive.org/story/2018-fair-elections-in-berkeley/) to 10 percent of total fundraising that year, down from 33 percent in 2016.

Proposition 4 comes at a critical time, both in California and nationally, when the public is profoundly angry (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/07/extraordinary-amount-money-pouring-into-midterm-elections/) about the impact of wealth in American politics. A majority of Americans (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/09/poll-americans-say-too-much-money-in-politics-00912455) across the ideological spectrum say that there is too much money in politics. They're fed up with corruption in government and broadly support (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/poll-voters-want-solutions-government-corruption) major reforms to fix our campaign finance system. It's hardly surprising, then, that a recent poll (https://www.ppic.org/blog/commentary-affordability-is-the-top-issue-on-californias-november-ballot/) of California voters named threats to democracy as the most pertinent issue facing the country.
Americans across the country recognize the problem with the dominance of unchecked wealth in our elections. Proposition 4 presents Californians with an opportunity to shift course and build momentum for more ambitious change nationwide.
